newsitem.title: UK: Russia military deteriorates, mutiny unlikely - IISS.
newsitem.headline: Russia military deteriorates, mutiny unlikely - IISS.

text.p: Russia's under-funded and demoralised armed forces will continue to deteriorate in 1997 but there is little chance of an army mutiny, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said on Wednesday.
"The decline in capability in all departments of the Russian armed forces seems set to continue," the IISS said in its annual report on the state of the world's armed forces.
The former Soviet armed forces swallowed vast sums during the Cold War but, since the break-up of the Communist superpower, both military spending and effectiveness have plunged.
President Boris Yeltsin expressed concern about the state of the armed forces last week, and security chief Alexander Lebed has said there is a danger of a mutiny in the army.

But IISS deputy director Rose Gottemoeller said that, although the military was in very poor shape, Lebed's comments should be seen in the light of disagreements between the defence and finance ministries as next year's budget was being drawn up.

"The armed forces are voting with their feet and (Defence Minister) General (Igor) Rodionov is worried about the number of men joining the commercial sector. Troops are selling their weapons," she told a news conference.
"It's an extremely serious problem, but there are no signs that troops will drive into the Kremlin in tanks...Russia is not facing a planned mutiny," she said.

The IISS report estimated that 1995 military expenditure fell by 15 percent over 1994 to $82 billion, saying real decline since 1992 had been 45 percent. Despite this, Russia remained the second largest military spender after the United States.
The disastrous Chechen war, in which Russian troops have been continually out-thought and out-fought by bands of lightly-armed rebels, shows how far the rot has set in.

"The best the Russian armed forces can now do is contain rebel military action, in particular to try to retain control of the larger population centres and the seat of government in the province, until a longer-term political solution is found," the report said.
"Unless the Russian military can improve its joint force operations, and engage the rebels in direct hand-to hand combat, it will be hard-pressed to achieve even that modest objective."
The IISS was unimpressed by plans to adopt a new military doctrine based on mobile rapid reaction forces to replace the huge World War Two-era formations so favoured in Soviet times.
"Organisational changes to develop more mobile formations suitable for operations both within Russia and outside have not been put into effect," said the report.
But Gottemoeller said it would be wrong to write the Russians off completely.
"They are making a great effort to keep themselves out there. Their strategic nuclear forces are being kept at operational readiness," she said.
"They have pulled out all the stops to get a naval force out on the high seas, to show the Russian people that they are still in the game. It helps to build morale."

The report doubted Yeltsin's promise to end conscription by the year 2000, saying the system of employing professional soldiers on contracts was proving expensive and attracting the wrong kind of people.
Lack of spending meant large parts of the air force were in a lamentable state, it said.
